documents.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools and Sample Syllabus Policy Statements
documents.stance_why: The page "recommends that instructors include a policy in all their syllabi" and offers three sample degrees ("Restrictive, Supervised and Permissive") for instructors to choose from or modify, setting no single university rule; it prefers teaching AI use over banning ("Rather than banning these tools"). This is delegation to instructors with tiers.
documents.summary: The Provost page recommends that every syllabus carry a generative AI statement and groups sample statements into Restrictive, Supervised and Permissive tiers. It adds advice on learning-first framing, instructor transparency, FERPA, and why AI detectors should not be sole evidence, and gives samples from Chicago, UT Austin, Harvard, the UMKC Conservatory, First Year Composition and Computer Science.

units.why: The provost says UMKC "recommends that instructors include a policy in all their syllabi", a syllabus-statement expectation addressed to instructors, so P09 (statement in every syllabus).
units.anchor: UMKC recommends that instructors include a policy in all their syllabi
units.fit_note: Phrased as a recommendation, not a requirement.

units.why: "Rather than banning these tools, faculty are encouraged to create AI policies that teach students how to use them ethically and effectively" favors teaching AI use over bans; P44 (teach effective AI use) fits better than P02 because the target is instructors designing policies.
units.anchor: faculty are encouraged to create AI policies that teach students how to use them
units.fit_note: Also discourages blanket bans, which P44 does not state. | Encourages faculty to write policies that teach ethical, effective use instead of banning; it is not a blanket student permission.
units.resolution_why: A coded P44 (teach students to use AI ethically), B coded P02 (default permit). The passage says "Rather than banning these tools, faculty are encouraged to create AI policies that teach students how to use them ethically and effectively". It is addressed to faculty policy design and sets no default permission for students, so P02 (default rule allows AI) does not fit; teaching effective AI use (P44) is what the sentence asks for. Final P44, with the anti-ban part kept as a fit_note.

units.why: "Having a clear policy ensures students understand expectations" gives the reason for a syllabus statement; it explains the P09 rule and adds no new rule, so informs.
units.anchor: Having a clear policy ensures students understand expectations
units.resolution_why: Found only by B. "Having a clear policy ensures students understand expectations" is a rationale for the syllabus-statement recommendation in the passage, so it is a real (informs) statement; kept as P09.

units.why: "Instructors should clearly communicate their policy to students and engage in regular discussions about generative AI use" goes beyond listing a rule in the syllabus, so P66 (explain and discuss) fits; P09 covers only stating it.
units.anchor: engage in regular discussions about generative AI use, particularly before major assignments

units.why: The page sorts sample statements into "three degrees of AI use permissions: Restrictive, Supervised and Permissive", i.e. named tiers, so P05.
units.anchor: three degrees of AI use permissions: Restrictive, Supervised and Permissive

units.why: Defines the Restrictive tier: policies "require students to complete all assignments without the use of GenAI", a named tier definition so P05 (not P01, because it describes one option among three).
units.anchor: require students to complete all assignments without the use of GenAI
units.resolution_why: Actor and phase differed (A instructor/before-course, B student/general). Tier definitions describe what a policy requires of students, but the sentence is guidance to instructors choosing a tier on a page for instructors, and the tiers are chosen when the course policy is designed. Final actor instructor and phase before-course, as for the other tier units.

units.why: Defines the Supervised tier: policies "allow students to complete assignments with GenAI according to the instructor's directions", a named tier definition so P05.
units.anchor: allow students to complete assignments with GenAI according to the instructor’s directions
units.resolution_why: Actor and phase differed (A instructor/before-course, B student/general). Tier definitions describe what a policy requires of students, but the sentence is guidance to instructors choosing a tier on a page for instructors, and the tiers are chosen when the course policy is designed. Final actor instructor and phase before-course, as for the other tier units.

units.why: Says supervised policies "may require that students acknowledge the use of GenAI, such as submitting inputs and outputs with assignments, citation practices, writing a memo"; this is disclosure with submissions, P24, with logs and memos as examples (P26 is narrower).
units.anchor: may require that students acknowledge the use of GenAI
units.fit_note: Also names submitting inputs and outputs and a memo on how GenAI was used (P26 elements), as options an instructor may choose.
units.resolution_why: Phase differed (A before-course, B course-start) and unit_stance (A permit, B require). The sentence says supervised policies "may require that students acknowledge the use of GenAI"; it tells instructors what they can build into a policy, so before-course. Unit_stance describes the position on AI use, and the supervised tier allows AI with acknowledgement, so permit; B's require would read as AI use being required.

units.why: Defines the Permissive tier: policies "allow students to complete assignments using GenAI as a close collaborator without instructor directions" and "may not require documentation", a named tier so P05.
units.anchor: allow students to complete assignments using GenAI as a close collaborator without instructor directions
units.resolution_why: Actor/phase differed (see tier units: final instructor, before-course) and unit_stance (A encourage, B permit). The text says permissive policies "allow students to complete assignments using GenAI as a close collaborator"; it allows and does not recommend, so permit. Tier definitions describe what a policy requires of students, but the sentence is guidance to instructors choosing a tier on a page for instructors, and the tiers are chosen when the course policy is designed. Final actor instructor and phase before-course, as for the other tier units.

units.why: Permissive policies "may not require documentation or acknowledgement that GenAI was used" says disclosure can be waived under the open tier. It is about disclosure, but P28 is about consequences; P24 is the nearest home since it states whether acknowledgement is required.
units.anchor: may not require documentation or acknowledgement that GenAI was used
units.fit_note: States that disclosure may be waived under the permissive tier, the opposite of requiring it.
units.resolution_why: Found only by B, from the same sentence as the permissive tier definition. "may not require documentation or acknowledgement that GenAI was used" is a separate rule (disclosure may be waived), so kept as P24 with its fit_note. Phase set to before-course (B had course-start) because it describes what a tier policy may include, like the other tier units.

units.why: "Determine which category your syllabus may fit under. Also consider if you will have a range of these policy types across different assignments" leaves the choice to the instructor and per assignment, so P04.
units.anchor: consider if you will have a range of these policy types across different assignments

units.why: Suggests "the AI Assessment Scale (AIAS) to develop ranges of GenAI use or non-use", pointing to a graded scale of use levels, so P05.
units.anchor: Consider using the AI Assessment Scale (AIAS) to develop ranges of GenAI use or non-use
units.fit_note: Recommends an external scale rather than defining the tiers itself.

units.why: "For guidance on creating your own syllabus statement, you can find helpful information compiled by UM System Academic Technologies" directs instructors to institutional support for writing policy, P63.
units.anchor: you can find helpful information compiled by
units.frag_start: For guidance on creating your own syllabus
units.fit_note: A pointer to UM System resources rather than workshops or consultations.
units.resolution_why: Found only by B. "For guidance on creating your own syllabus statement, you can find helpful information compiled by UM System Academic Technologies" points instructors to institutional support for writing policy, a real if mild statement; kept as P63 with a fit_note because it is a pointer rather than workshops.

units.why: "Lead with learning outcomes and disciplinary values, not with the motivation to curb cheating" ties the AI decision to learning goals, so P83 (align AI decisions with learning objectives).
units.anchor: Lead with learning outcomes and disciplinary values, not with the motivation to curb cheating
units.fit_note: Also says to lead with learning rather than cheating prevention and that integrity is a tool for inquiry.

units.why: "Consider if GenAI can scaffold or not scaffold learning in these areas" asks instructors to decide AI use by whether it supports learning, P83 again; kept as a separate unit because it states a second test (scaffolding).
units.anchor: Consider if GenAI can scaffold or not scaffold learning in these areas

units.why: "be transparent with students about how you use GenAI" in lesson plans, questions and assignments is instructor disclosure to students, P47 (P48 would be about reviewing materials, which is not stated).
units.anchor: be transparent with students about how you use GenAI
units.fit_note: Applies to AI used to create lesson plans, discussion questions and assignments, justified by reciprocity with student transparency.

units.why: "Do not upload or copy and paste student work into any GenAI product to help with assessment, as this may violate FERPA" bars instructors from sharing student data with AI; nearest is P50 (protect personal data), though it is addressed to instructors assessing work.
units.anchor: Do not upload or copy and paste student work into any GenAI product
units.fit_note: Also limits AI-assisted assessment of student work; P101 does not fit as no conditions are given. | Addressed to instructors (protecting student records under FERPA) and also limits AI-assisted assessment; P50 is about personal data protection.
units.resolution_why: Phase differed (A general, B during-work) and unit_stance (A restrict, B prohibit). "Do not upload or copy and paste student work into any GenAI product to help with assessment" is an unconditional bar on one use, so prohibit; it applies whenever instructors assess work and is not tied to a course phase, so general.

units.why: States detection tools "cannot provide clear evidence" and have "significant margins of error", so detectors are unreliable: P39.
units.anchor: cannot provide clear evidence that supports the case

units.why: Notes detectors "have also been shown to be biased against certain populations of students, such as non-native speakers", a further reason detectors are unreliable, so P39.
units.anchor: biased against certain populations of students, such as non-native speakers
units.fit_note: Concerns bias against non-native speakers, which P53 also touches; chosen P39 because it argues detector unreliability.
units.resolution_why: A coded P39, B coded P53. The sentence "Detection tools have also been shown to be biased against certain populations of students, such as non-native speakers" sits in the detection section and is another reason not to rely on detectors. A reader looking for the detector rule would look under P39; P53 is about bias of AI itself. Final P39, with B's reading kept in the fit_note.

units.why: "we do not recommend using these detection tools as the single piece of evidence to support a violation" makes detector output only supporting evidence, which is P69 (evidence standards); P39 says detectors are not relied on at all.
units.anchor: we do not recommend using these detection tools as the single piece

units.why: The Chicago sample says "students are not allowed to use any AI tools, such as ChatGPT or DallE 2, in this course", a blanket course ban: P01.
units.anchor: students are not allowed to use any AI tools, such as ChatGPT or DallE 2
units.fit_note: Sample statement quoted from the University of Chicago, hosted as a model by the UMKC Provost.

units.why: "we will be developing skills and knowledge that are important to discover and practice on your own", together with the claim that AI tools inhibit them, gives the skill-building reason for the ban: P41.
units.anchor: important to discover and practice on your own
units.fit_note: Sample statement quoted from the University of Chicago.

units.why: "Students are expected to present work that is their own without assistance from others, including automated tools" states ownership of submitted work: P29.
units.anchor: present work that is their own without assistance from others, including automated tools
units.fit_note: Sample statement quoted from the University of Chicago.
units.resolution_why: Modality (A must, B should) and unit_stance (A prohibit, B restrict). "Students are expected to present work that is their own without assistance from others, including automated tools" is in a statement banning all AI, and "are expected" is a binding expectation, so must; with automated tools excluded it is a prohibition.

units.why: "If you are unclear if something is an AI tool, please check with your instructor" tells students to ask when unsure: P10.
units.anchor: If you are unclear if something is an AI tool, please check with your instructor
units.fit_note: Sample from the University of Chicago; unsure about whether a tool counts as AI.

units.why: "Using AI tools for any purpose in this course will violate the university's academic integrity policy" classifies use as an integrity violation: P36.
units.anchor: Using AI tools for any purpose in this course will violate the university’s academic integrity
units.fit_note: Sample statement quoted from the University of Chicago.

units.why: UT Austin sample: "All assignments should be fully prepared by the student" states that the student must own the work, P29.
units.anchor: All assignments should be fully prepared by the student
units.frag_start: All assignments should be fully prepared
units.fit_note: Sample statement quoted from UT Austin.
units.resolution_why: Found only by B. "All assignments should be fully prepared by the student" is the UT Austin sample's ownership rule (P29) and is distinct from the ban sentence and the plagiarism sentence; kept. Unit_stance set to prohibit (B had restrict) because in this restrictive sample it excludes any AI preparation.

units.why: "Developing strong competencies ... will prepare you for success in your degree pathway and, ultimately, a competitive career" gives career readiness as the reason for the ban; P94 (careers as a reason to build skills without AI) fits.
units.anchor: will prepare you for success in your degree pathway and, ultimately, a competitive career
units.fit_note: Combined with skill development; sample from UT Austin.

units.why: "the use of generative AI tools to complete any aspect of assignments for this course is not permitted" is a default ban on graded work: P01 (the plagiarism label in the same sentence is not split out).
units.anchor: generative AI tools to complete any aspect of assignments for this course is not permitted
units.fit_note: Also says violations are treated as plagiarism (P36). | Sample statement quoted from UT Austin.

units.why: UT Austin sample: "will be treated as plagiarism" puts the banned AI use under plagiarism, P36.
units.anchor: will be treated as plagiarism
units.frag_start: Therefore, the use of generative AI
units.fit_note: Sample statement quoted from UT Austin.
units.resolution_why: Found only by B. "will be treated as plagiarism" states the consequence of the ban in the UT Austin sample; A mentioned it only in a fit_note. It is a separate rule (classification of misuse) so kept as P36.

units.why: "If you have questions about what constitutes a violation of this statement, please contact me" tells students to ask the instructor: P10.
units.anchor: If you have questions about what constitutes a violation of this statement, please contact me
units.fit_note: Sample statement quoted from UT Austin.

units.why: The second UT sample says brainstorming and "exploring possible responses to questions or problems" with AI "may be useful", encouraging that use: P15.
units.anchor: brainstorming ideas, exploring possible responses to questions or problems
units.fit_note: Sample statement quoted from UT Austin; also mentions creative engagement with materials.

units.why: "Please feel free to reach out to me well in advance of the due date of assignments for which you may be using generative AI tools" asks students to consult the instructor before use: P10.
units.anchor: reach out to me well in advance of the due date of assignments
units.fit_note: Sample statement quoted from UT Austin; sample is permissive in tone yet defers acceptability to discussion.

units.why: The Conservatory says "we value the messy work of creation over the digital sheen of perfection provided by AI technology", a rationale for limiting AI to protect human creative work, P41 as nearest; it is about values and voice rather than skill-building alone.
units.anchor: We value the messy work of creation over the digital sheen of perfection
units.frag_start: At the UMKC Conservatory, we believe
units.fit_note: Grounds the limit in human voice and creativity rather than skill practice. | Rationale is about human creativity and students' distinctive voices, not only skill-building.
units.resolution_why: Actor and phase differed (A student/course-start, B all/general). The Conservatory values statement ("We value the messy work of creation over the digital sheen of perfection") is an institutional principle, not an instruction to students at the start of a course. Final all/general.

units.why: "we welcome the exploration of generative AI tools under the following guidelines" permits AI with conditions as the Conservatory default: P02.
units.anchor: we welcome the exploration of generative AI tools under the following guidelines

units.why: "Students must be the primary author of any submitted work" keeps the student as principal thinker/author, P32.
units.anchor: Students must be the primary author of any submitted work.
units.fit_note: Speaks of authorship rather than problem solving.
units.resolution_why: Unit_stance differed (A permit, B restrict). "Students must be the primary author of any submitted work" is a condition limiting how AI may be used, so restrict.

units.why: "Students must properly cite the use of generative AI tools" requires acknowledgement of AI use: P24.
units.anchor: Students must properly cite the use of generative AI tools.
units.resolution_why: Unit_stance differed (A permit, B require). The unit_stance field records the position on AI use; requiring citation of AI use is a condition on permitted use, so permit. B's require would mean AI use is required.

units.why: "Students must not use AI to bypass key learning objectives of the class" bans AI use that undercuts learning goals; nearest P83 (align with learning objectives), though here it is a prohibition on students.
units.anchor: Students must not use AI to bypass key learning objectives of the class.
units.fit_note: A student-facing prohibition, whereas P83 is about how decisions are made.
units.resolution_why: A coded P83, B coded UNCOVERED. P83 covers that whether and how AI is allowed should follow from learning objectives. "Students must not use AI to bypass key learning objectives of the class" says exactly that, as a student-facing limit, so it fits P83 with a fit_note; no new type is needed.

units.why: "Students must obtain permission for AI use in each class project" makes permission project by project, so the rule is set per assignment: P04.
units.anchor: Students must obtain permission for AI use in each class project.
units.fit_note: Gives the student a duty to seek permission, not just says who decides.

units.why: "Students should be mindful of the shortcomings of such tools and understand that the information they provide might not be accurate" says to treat output as fallible: P31.
units.anchor: the information they provide might not be accurate

units.why: The First Year Composition Committee "invites students to use LLMs like ChatGPT as tools best suited for integration into your writing process", an invitation to use AI for writing, P91.
units.anchor: invites students to use LLMs like ChatGPT as tools best suited for integration
units.frag_start: The UMKC First Year Composition Committee
units.fit_note: Sample from UMKC English Language and Literatures.
units.resolution_why: A coded P02, B coded P91. The Committee "invites students to use LLMs like ChatGPT as tools best suited for integration into your writing process"; the permission is specifically for writing support, which is what P91 covers. P02 is a course-wide default and is not what is stated. Final P91.

units.why: "you may not use LLMs to create whole or partially generated text ... that takes the place of your original writing" bans AI-produced submitted text: P19.
units.anchor: you may not use LLMs to create whole or partially generated text

units.why: "Doing so would count as plagiarism according to the University of Missouri System Academic Conduct on unauthorized use of generative AI" classifies it as misconduct: P36.
units.anchor: Doing so would count as plagiarism

units.why: The list under "Using LLMs to support the writing process includes:" names uses of AI that are allowed for writing (ideas, research, thesis statements, other arguments, first drafts for revision, style feedback). P91 (allow AI for writing support) is the permission itself; P18 is about treating prose differently from code and does not state this list.
units.anchor: Using LLMs to support the writing process includes:
units.policy: Using LLMs to support the writing process includes generating ideas, conducting research, generating thesis statements, discovering other arguments and perspectives, generating first drafts for in-depth revision and extension, and improving writing style and other global and local issues as a peer reviewer.
units.fit_note: The anchor is the list lead-in; the listed uses follow it in the source. | Also includes generating ideas and research (P15) and AI first drafts, which sits uneasily with the stated ban on AI text replacing original writing.
units.resolution_why: A coded P18, B coded P91. P18 covers separating prose rules from code rules; the list is a permission for AI help in writing, which P91 defines. Final P91. Anchor kept as the list lead-in with the normalized policy listing the uses.

units.why: "I may use class time to guide you in using LLMs for your writing process or assign work that has you deploy LLMs" says AI use may be built into assignments: P79.
units.anchor: assign work that has you deploy LLMs for your writing process
units.fit_note: Also says class time may be used to teach LLM use (P44).

units.why: "We may also discuss the limitations and harms of these technologies, such as making up facts ... and showing bias against marginalized communities' linguistic practices" names harms and limits, P53 (P31 covers only verification).
units.anchor: We may also discuss the limitations and harms of these technologies
units.frag_start: We may also discuss the limitations
units.fit_note: Also covers fabrication, which P31 addresses. | Also notes fabricated facts and sources (P31).
units.resolution_why: Modality differed (A informs, B may). "We may also discuss the limitations and harms of these technologies" says what the instructor may do in class, so may; the content is P53.

units.why: "It is important to consult me before using them in an assignment" asks students to check with the instructor first when no specific instruction is given: P10.
units.anchor: It is important to consult me
units.fit_note: Applies when the instructor gave no specific AI instruction; also acts as a fallback rule (P06).
units.resolution_why: Unit_stance differed (A neutral, B restrict). Asking the instructor first is a procedure and does not itself allow or limit AI, so neutral.

units.why: "cite them in your Works Cited page" requires acknowledging AI use in the submission: P24.
units.anchor: cite them in your Works Cited page
units.fit_note: Same sentence also requires a rationale (separate unit). | Also requires students to argue a rationale for appropriateness (P30-like).
units.resolution_why: Both coded P24 with a fit_note. B put the rationale duty in the same unit; A split it into a second unit (below). This unit keeps the citation duty only. Unit_stance permit (B said require) since citation is a condition on permitted use.

units.why: "be prepared to argue a rationale for the appropriateness of their use" requires students to justify AI use; no type covers a duty to justify, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: be prepared to argue a rationale for the appropriateness of their use
units.uncovered_note: Students must be ready to argue why their AI use was appropriate.
units.resolution_why: Found only by A. "be prepared to argue a rationale for the appropriateness of their use" is a separate duty (justify AI use) from citing it. P30 covers explaining what one submits, not defending the use of AI, so UNCOVERED is kept. B folded it into its P24 unit with a fit_note.

units.why: "You will be expected to include the chat history with the LLM as evidence of your writing process" requires a transcript: P26.
units.anchor: include the chat history with the LLM as evidence of your writing process
units.resolution_why: Unit_stance differed (A permit, B require). Submitting the chat history is a condition on permitted use, so permit.

units.why: Says sharing LLM use "allows the writing program to develop policies that meet the needs of students and instructors" and track technology change: student disclosures feed policy revision, P55 nearest.
units.anchor: develop policies that meet the needs of students and instructors
units.fit_note: Collects student experience to shape policy, not evidence of learning effects. | Also says the writing program uses student accounts to develop its policies (P54).
units.resolution_why: Actor differed (A student, B all). The sentence tells students that sharing their LLM use helps the writing program develop policies; the people bound are students. Final student, P55 with fit_note.

units.why: "The only way you can be punished for using LLMs is if you keep it to yourself and pretend that you generated the content" makes nondisclosure the violation and disclosed use safe: P28.
units.anchor: The only way you can be punished for using LLMs is if you keep it

units.why: Harvard sample 1: "Certain assignments in this course will permit or even encourage the use of generative artificial intelligence" lets permission vary by assignment, P04.
units.anchor: Certain assignments in this course will permit or even encourage
units.frag_start: Certain assignments in this course will
units.fit_note: Sample from Harvard.
units.resolution_why: Found only by B. "Certain assignments in this course will permit or even encourage the use of generative artificial intelligence" says permission varies by assignment (P04); distinct from the default sentence that follows. Modality informs, unit_stance permit.

units.why: "The default is that such use is disallowed unless otherwise stated" is the fallback when a course says nothing: P06.
units.anchor: The default is that such use is disallowed unless otherwise stated.
units.fit_note: Sample from Harvard College hosted by the UMKC Provost; applies to course assignments generally.

units.why: "Any such use must be appropriately acknowledged and cited" (Harvard sample) requires disclosure: P24.
units.anchor: Any such use must be appropriately acknowledged and cited.
units.fit_note: Sample from Harvard.
units.resolution_why: Unit_stance differed (A permit, B require). Acknowledging and citing AI use is a condition on permitted use, so permit; require would mean AI use is required.

units.why: "It is each student's responsibility to assess the validity and applicability of any GAI output ... you bear the final responsibility" requires verifying output: P31.
units.anchor: responsibility to assess the validity and applicability of any GAI output
units.fit_note: Also says the student bears final responsibility (P29). | Also says students bear final responsibility (P29). Sample from Harvard.
units.resolution_why: Unit_stance differed (A permit, B restrict). Responsibility to check output is a condition on permitted use and does not itself limit AI, so permit.

units.why: Harvard sample 1: "Violations of this policy will be considered academic misconduct" classes violations as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: Violations of this policy will be considered academic misconduct.
units.frag_start: Violations of this policy will be
units.fit_note: Sample from Harvard.
units.resolution_why: Unit_stance differed (A neutral, B restrict). Violations of the policy being misconduct is an enforcement rule that backs the limits in the sample, so restrict.

units.why: "different classes at Harvard could implement different AI policies, and it is the student's responsibility to conform to expectations for each course" makes students learn and follow each course's rules: P78.
units.anchor: it is the student’s responsibility to conform to expectations for each course
units.fit_note: Also says policies differ by class (P11). | Also says courses differ (P11). Sample from Harvard.

units.why: The second Harvard sample "encourages students to explore the use of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) tools such as ChatGPT for all assignments and assessments", encouraging AI by default: P02.
units.anchor: This course encourages students to explore the use of generative artificial intelligence
units.fit_note: Sample from Harvard; includes assessments.
units.resolution_why: Phase differed (A during-work, B course-start). The sentence encourages exploring AI for all assignments and assessments; it governs the work itself, so during-work.

units.why: The UMKC CS sample says "there is no limitation on the use of generative AI for brainstorming, developing ideas, drafting responses for homework", a permissive default: P02.
units.anchor: there is no limitation on the use of generative AI for brainstorming, developing ideas
units.fit_note: Also names brainstorming (P15) and drafting homework responses (P16-like). Layer is the Provost page quoting a School of Science and Engineering CS statement.
units.resolution_why: Topics differ; B added code-generation but the passage mentions no code. Final topics from A.

units.why: "such use must be documented to a degree of detail specified in the assignment" requires disclosure with the work: P24.
units.anchor: such use must be documented to a degree of detail specified in the assignment
units.fit_note: Level of detail is set per assignment.
units.resolution_why: Unit_stance differed (A permit, B require). Documenting AI use is a condition on the permitted use in the CS sample, so permit; require would mean AI use is required.

units.why: "these tools often produce inaccurate or incorrect answers and ... should not be relied upon as search engines" warns of errors, P31.
units.anchor: these tools often produce inaccurate or incorrect answers
units.frag_start: these tools often produce inaccurate or incorrect
units.resolution_why: Modality differed (A should-not, B informs). The anchored clause "these tools often produce inaccurate or incorrect answers" is a fact; the "should not be relied upon as search engines" clause is in the same sentence. Final informs with the factual clause as anchor.

units.why: "You are still responsible for the accuracy and correctness of anything you submit" makes students own what they submit: P29.
units.anchor: You are still responsible for the accuracy and correctness of anything you submit
units.resolution_why: Unit_stance differed (A neutral, B restrict). Being responsible for what you submit places no limit on AI use by itself, so neutral.

units.why: "such tools can generate responses that are stereotyped, racist, sexist or otherwise biased" names bias harms: P53.
units.anchor: responses that are stereotyped, racist, sexist or otherwise biased

units.why: "These tools are particularly poor at assessing the quality of their own responses" warns that AI cannot check its own output: P31.
units.anchor: These tools are particularly poor at assessing the quality of their own responses.
units.resolution_why: Found only by A. "These tools are particularly poor at assessing the quality of their own responses" is a separate warning about reliability from the inaccuracy sentence; kept as P31.

units.why: "Failure to document use of these tools will be considered academic dishonesty" makes nondisclosure the violation: P28.
units.anchor: Failure to document use of these tools will be considered academic dishonesty.
units.resolution_why: Unit_stance differed (A neutral, B require). Failing to document being academic dishonesty is an enforcement rule, so neutral.

units.why: "prompts used with these systems are to be your own unaided work" sets a rule that prompts must be written by the student; no type covers this, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: prompts used with these systems are to be your own unaided work
units.uncovered_note: Prompts given to AI must be the student's own unaided work.
units.resolution_why: Found only by A. "prompts used with these systems are to be your own unaided work" is a rule about who writes the prompts, separate from the submission rule that follows. No type covers it, so UNCOVERED is kept; B mentioned it only in a fit_note.

units.why: "you may be required to submit your prompts as part of your deliverables" allows requiring prompts with the work: P25 (prompts) fits, P26 (logs) less specifically.
units.anchor: you may be required to submit your prompts as part of your deliverables
